title: Same honest score, same false alarms?
hook: One risk score is equally accurate for two groups. Who gets wrongly flagged?

knows: that a calibrated score means '80% means 80%' (say-seventy-mean-it)
doesNotKnow: that when two groups have different base rates, one calibrated score with one threshold must give them different false-alarm and miss rates, so 'fair' has to pick which equality it means

misconception: If a risk score is equally accurate (calibrated) for both groups and uses one threshold, it treats both groups' innocent people the same.
objective: The learner can explain that a score calibrated in two groups with different base rates flags a larger share of the higher-base-rate group's innocent people, and that the error rates match only when the base rates match.

claims.text: In the toy, in both groups 80% of the people labelled high risk (ringed) and 20% of the others reoffend (the question and the stage message: '8 in 10 ringed dots reoffended, in A and in B').
claims.source: By construction: reoffends(i, high) in Demo.tsx marks 4 in 5 of the ringed and 1 in 5 of the others by the pattern (i + row) % 5; exact for every slider value (multiples of 5). node: ringed reoffenders 40 of 50 (A), 16 of 20, 4 of 5, 28 of 35, 40 of 50 (B at 20, 5, 35, 50).

claims.text: Group A (50 ringed): false alarms 10 of 50 non-reoffenders (20%), misses 10 of 50 reoffenders (20%). Group B with 20 ringed: false alarms 4 of 68 (5.9%, shown 6%), misses 16 of 32 (50%).
claims.source: rates() in Demo.tsx; node 2026-10-14 matches brief 56 (company/domains/briefs/ai.ai-society.md). Other slider values: B at 5 ringed 1 of 77 (1%) and 19 of 23 (83%); at 35 ringed 7 of 59 (12%) and 13 of 41 (32%).

claims.text: A has more reoffenders, so more of A sits in the ringed rows; the two groups' false-alarm and miss rates are equal only when B has 50 ringed, where B's base rate matches A's (50%).
claims.source: Slider sweep 5/20/35/50 (node, rates()): B false alarms 1.3/5.9/11.9/20.0%, misses 82.6/50.0/31.7/20.0%; A is 20.0/20.0. Reoffenders in B: 23/32/41/50 of 100.

claims.text: With different base rates, no imperfect score is both calibrated and equal on both errors (false-positive and false-negative rates) across groups.
claims.source: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017), 'Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores', ITCS 2017 (arXiv 1609.05807); Chouldechova (2017), 'Fair prediction with disparate impact', Big Data 5(2): 153-163, eq. 2.1: FPR = p/(1-p) * (1-PPV)/PPV * (1-FNR); toy check A: 1 * 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2, B: 0.32/0.68 * 0.25 * 0.5 = 0.0588. About real systems; needs the fact-checker.

claims.text: The two groups, their sizes and the 80%/20% rates are a toy, labelled on the stage ('Toy groups of 100'); which dots reoffend is a fixed pattern, not a chosen seed.
claims.source: Brief 56 in company/domains/briefs/ai.ai-society.md. The optional COMPAS sentence (brief claim 5) is not in learner text.

recall.question: A loan-default score is calibrated for two towns: '30% risk' means 30% default in both. Town X has many more defaulters. Using one cut-off, what happens to people who would have repaid?
options: A larger share of X's repayers are refused
Both towns' repayers are refused at the same rate
A larger share of the other town's repayers are refused
recall.why: More of X's people get high scores, so more of X's repayers land above the cut-off too. With different base rates a calibrated score cannot also equalise false alarms.
